f: Distinguish a secured bond from a debenture.
b:
Secured bond — pledges specific assets that bondholders can sell if the issuer misses interest or principal.
Debenture — unsecured; backed only by the issuer's credit and reputation, so it yields more than a secured bond of the same issuer and term.
A subordinated debenture ranks behind other creditors and pays more still, yet sits ahead of common stock.

f: What three drawbacks does a call feature create for the bondholder?
b:
• Cash flows are uncertain (the bond may disappear early).
  • Calls happen after rates drop, so proceeds are reinvested at lower rates (reinvestment risk).
  • Price gains are capped: the bond rarely trades far above its call price once a call is expected.
Issuers call to refinance at a lower coupon; corporate indentures generally give at least 10 years of call protection.

f: Where is the dividing line between investment-grade and high-yield (junk) bonds?
b:
Investment grade = the top four categories: BBB− or better (S&P) or Baa or better (Moody's).
Below that (BB+ / Ba and lower) is noninvestment grade, with higher default risk and higher yields. Some institutions may buy only investment-grade issues.

f: Distinguish interest rate risk from reinvestment rate risk.
b:
Interest rate risk — rates rise → the fixed cash flows are discounted at a higher rate → price falls.
Reinvestment rate risk — rates fall → coupons (and returned principal) are reinvested at lower rates, so the realized return can fall short of the promised YTM.
They pull in opposite directions; for exam purposes a zero-coupon bond has no reinvestment rate risk.

f: What are Treasury STRIPS, and why are they best held in a tax-deferred account?
b:
Zero-coupon bonds made by separating each coupon and the principal of a T-note or T-bond into its own security. Bought through brokers, dealers and institutions (not from the Treasury), at a deep discount; very rate-sensitive, no call risk, virtually no default or liquidity risk.
Tax: interest is taxed as ordinary income as it accrues even though no cash is paid (phantom income) → tax-deferred account.

f: How do TIPS protect against inflation, and how is the inflation adjustment taxed?
b:
Principal is indexed to the CPI. Each six months the payment = adjusted principal × (fixed coupon rate ÷ 2), so the rate stays fixed but the dollar coupon moves. At maturity the holder gets the greater of original or adjusted principal.
Tax: interest and any upward principal adjustment are federal ordinary income in the year they occur (adjustment raises basis); no state or local income tax.

f: Which agency securities have the direct backing of the U.S. government, and which only indirect backing?
b:
Direct: GNMA (Ginnie Mae) and the Farm Credit Administration.
Indirect: FHLMC (Freddie Mac), FNMA (Fannie Mae), SLMA (Sallie Mae) — so they pay slightly higher coupons.
Unlike Treasuries, agency interest is generally taxable at federal, state and local levels. (Fannie and Freddie have been in FHFA conservatorship since 2008.)

f: Distinguish prepayment risk from extension risk in mortgage pass-throughs.
b:
Prepayment risk — rates fall → homeowners refinance → principal returns early and must be reinvested at lower rates; price gains are limited (an embedded call).
Extension risk — rates rise → prepayments slow → average life lengthens and expected principal arrives later, lowering the return.

f: Distinguish general obligation (GO) bonds from revenue bonds.
b:
GO bonds — fund projects that earn no revenue; repaid from the municipality's taxes (full faith and credit); usually need voter approval; debt limits protect holders → lower risk.
Revenue bonds — repaid only from the income of the financed facility (e.g., an airport) → riskier, so higher yields for similar maturities.

f: What is the taxable equivalent yield (TEY) formula, and when do you use it?
b:
TEY = tax-exempt yield ÷ (1 − marginal tax rate)
Use it to restate a muni yield as the taxable yield a corporate bond must beat. The mirror formula is after-tax yield = taxable yield × (1 − marginal rate).
The higher the bracket, the bigger the edge for tax-exempt income.

f: Distinguish original issue discount (OID) from market discount for tax purposes.
b:
OID — issued below par. A computed slice of the discount is income every year (phantom income), and basis rises by that amount.
Market discount — issued at par but bought later below par because its value fell. Generally not taxed until sale or maturity, then treated as interest income; only gain beyond the accrued market discount is capital gain. (An election to accrue it yearly exists but is rarely used.)

f: Which client need do zero-coupon bonds fit best, and what is their main tax drawback?
b:
Fit: a known sum on a known date (e.g., tuition) — no reinvestment rate risk, and the deep discount buys more face value per dollar.
Drawback: taxable zeros create phantom income — accrued interest is taxed yearly though no cash arrives → hold in a retirement or other tax-deferred account. Prices are also more volatile than coupon bonds of similar quality.

f: Distinguish Yankee bonds, Eurodollar bonds, and Eurobonds.
b:
Yankee — foreign issuer, U.S.-dollar denominated, sold and traded in the U.S. → no currency risk for a U.S. investor.
Eurodollar — U.S.-dollar bonds sold outside the U.S. by non-U.S. issuers through a non-U.S. syndicate; no SEC registration.
Eurobond — denominated in a currency not native to the country where issued (any currency, not just euros); sold by international syndicates.

f: What is the conversion ratio formula?
b:
Conversion ratio = par value ÷ conversion price
= the number of shares each bond converts into. The conversion price is the stock price at which the exchange happens.
E.g., $1,000 par ÷ $20 conversion price = 50 shares.

f: How do you calculate a convertible bond's conversion value?
b:
Conversion value = conversion ratio × current market price of the stock
It is what the bond would be worth if converted today. E.g., 50 shares × $23 = $1,150.

f: What is a convertible bond's investment value, and how is it found?
b:
Its value as a straight (nonconvertible) bond — the PV of the semiannual coupons plus par, discounted at the market rate for comparable straight bonds.
It is the cushion under the price if the stock collapses, and it moves whenever interest rates move.

f: What is the lowest price a convertible bond should trade for?
b: The greater of its investment (straight) value or its conversion value. If it traded below conversion value, buyers would snap it up and convert; below straight value, it would be cheap as a bond.

f: Distinguish the conversion premium from the investment premium.
b:
Conversion premium = market price − conversion value; % = ÷ conversion value. (Premium over the bond's worth as stock.)
Investment premium = market price − investment value; % = ÷ investment value. (Premium paid for the conversion option over its worth as a bond.)

f: How is a convertible's downside risk measured, and what is the classic percentage mistake?
b:
Dollar downside risk = market price − investment value (the same dollars as the investment premium).
Percentage downside risk = that difference ÷ market price — not ÷ investment value. It measures how far the price could fall from today's price to the straight-bond floor. It changes as rates change.

f: What is portfolio immunization, and when is the offset complete?
b:
A technique that sets price (interest rate) risk against reinvestment rate risk: if rates rise, prices fall but coupons reinvest higher, and vice versa.
Full offset when portfolio duration = duration of the liability (the investor's time horizon).
Not passive: portfolio duration drifts down faster than the liability's, so periodic rebalancing is needed.

f: How can a family immunize a known college bill with a single bond?
b:
Buy a zero-coupon bond maturing when the money is needed — a zero's duration equals its maturity, so duration matches the horizon exactly.
A coupon bond's duration is shorter than its maturity, so a coupon bond would need to mature somewhat after the target date.

f: What is a bond ladder, and what are its two advantages?
b:
Equal slices spread across staggered maturities (e.g., 1 through 5 years); each maturing rung is rolled to the long end.
  • Higher yield than an all-short-term portfolio.
  • Regular maturities supply cash to reinvest, keep the structure intact and limit damage from rising rates.
A long-term, relatively passive strategy.

f: How is a barbell structured, and why does it need active management?
b:
Only short-term and long-term bonds — nothing in the middle (also called a dumbbell). The long end locks in long rates; the short end keeps money free to use elsewhere if bonds fall.
Short bonds keep maturing, so proceeds must be redeployed to hold the shape → active management.

f: How does a bullet strategy work, and what is it designed to do?
b:
Bonds are bought at different times so that they all mature on one target date (e.g., an 8-year bond now, a 6-year in two years, a 4-year in four years).
Purpose: match duration to a single future cash need and minimize interest rate risk.

f: Distinguish a substitution swap from an intermarket spread swap.
b:
Substitution — swap into a bond with identical characteristics that is priced differently; a short-lived arbitrage until the market corrects.
Intermarket spread — swap between bond sectors (e.g., governments ↔ corporates) because one sector looks mispriced relative to the other; aims to exploit a YTM gap across markets.

f: A manager expects interest rates to rise. Which swap fits, and what does she do?
b: A rate anticipation swap: sell long-term bonds and buy short-term bonds to cut price sensitivity. If she expected rates to fall, she would do the reverse (short → long).

f: Which bond traits raise relative price swings, and how should a portfolio be built for a rate forecast?
b:
Bigger price swings come with a lower coupon, longer maturity and lower YTM.
Expect falling rates → long maturities, low coupons (maximum sensitivity, capture gains).
Expect rising rates → short maturities, high coupons (minimum sensitivity, limit losses).

f: Why should a newly retired couple not keep all of their bond money in T-bills?
b: Time horizon matters more than age. A 60- or 65-year-old may live 20+ more years, and a couple's joint horizon can be longer. With a horizon beyond about 10 years, the portfolio needs more than T-bills.

f: Why does the textbook suggest a TIPS ladder inside a traditional IRA for retirees?
b:
Staggered TIPS maturities deliver inflation-adjusted cash each year. Held to maturity they carry no default, call or interest rate risk and little purchasing power risk.
Inside a traditional IRA, the yearly inflation step-ups on unmatured bonds are not taxed currently (avoiding phantom income).

f: What does each yield curve shape typically signal?
b:
• Normal (upward) — economic expansion; rates expected to rise.
  • Flat — economy near a peak; little change in rates expected.
  • Inverted — Fed has tightened in an inflationary economy; rates expected to fall; may signal recession.
  • Humped — middle maturities yield the most.

f: Name the three yield curve theories, and say which one explains only an upward-sloping curve.
b:
Unbiased expectations, liquidity preference, and market segmentation.
Liquidity preference explains only a normal (upward) curve; the other two can explain any shape.

f: What does the unbiased expectations theory say, and what is its formula?
b:
Long-term rates are the geometric mean of today's short rate and expected future short rates.
1 + RN = [(1 + R1)(1 + E(r2)) … (1 + E(rN))]1/N
Expected higher short rates → upward curve; expected lower short rates → inverted curve.

f: What does the liquidity preference theory assume about investors?
b: Investors prefer short-term bonds (less price volatility, easier to turn into predictable cash), so they must be paid a liquidity premium to lend long. Result: the curve should slope upward; other shapes are temporary aberrations.

f: What drives the shape of the yield curve under market segmentation theory?
b: Supply and demand inside separate maturity segments. Institutions match assets to liabilities (banks lend short, savings and loans intermediate, life insurers long) and stay in their segment; in the strong form they never cross segments for extra yield. So the curve reflects institutional maturity needs and can take any shape.

f: With an inverted yield curve, why does the textbook favor long-term bonds over higher-yielding short-term paper?
b: When the curve returns to normal, all rates fall but short rates fall the most. Long bonds lock in the high rate and gain the most price; short paper simply matures and is reinvested at lower rates. Income buyers should insist on call protection.

f: Why is preferred stock called a hybrid security?
b:
Bond-like: fixed dividend set as a % of par; no vote; no share of profits; paid ahead of common; price moves inversely with rates.
Equity-like: the board must declare the dividend (not guaranteed); a missed dividend does not trigger bankruptcy; no maturity date (a perpetuity), so holders must sell to get their money back.

f: What does a cumulative feature give preferred shareholders?
b: Any skipped preferred dividends from prior years (arrears) must be paid, along with the current preferred dividend, before common shareholders receive any dividend.

f: How do you value a no-growth preferred stock, and why is it more rate-sensitive than the issuer's bonds?
b:
V = D ÷ r (a perpetuity: annual dividend ÷ required return or market yield on similar preferreds).
With no maturity date, its price swings more than the same company's bonds for a given rate change → buy in steady or falling rate environments.

f: What dividends-received deduction can a corporation take on preferred dividends it receives?
b: Subject to limits: 50% of dividends received if it owns less than 20% of the payer; 65% if it owns 20% or more (2026 edition figure). It applies to dividends from domestic corporations, not to bond interest.
